notes.definition: The human body defends itself against pathogens in two ways: non-specific defences (skin, nose, trachea and bronchi, stomach) that stop pathogens entering, and the immune system, in which white blood cells destroy pathogens that do get in.
explanation: The body's first line of defence is a set of non-specific defence systems. They are called non-specific because they act against any pathogen, not one particular type. Their job is to stop pathogens getting into the body. The four you need to know are the skin, the nose, the trachea and bronchi, and the stomach.

The skin covers the body and acts as a physical barrier that pathogens cannot easily get through. It also secretes antimicrobial substances that kill pathogens on its surface. If the skin is cut, pathogens can enter, which is why the blood clots quickly to seal wounds. The nose has hairs and produces mucus, which trap particles in the air that may contain pathogens, before they reach the lungs.

The trachea and bronchi (the airways to the lungs) are lined with cells that secrete mucus and with ciliated cells. The sticky mucus traps pathogens and dust. The cilia, which are tiny hair-like structures, beat to waft the mucus upwards to the back of the throat, where it is swallowed. The stomach produces hydrochloric acid, which kills most pathogens that are swallowed in food, drink or mucus.

If a pathogen does enter the body, the immune system tries to destroy it. White blood cells help to defend against pathogens in three ways. First, by phagocytosis: some white blood cells engulf (surround and take in) pathogens and digest them. Second, by producing antibodies. Antibodies are proteins that bind to specific antigens on the surface of a particular pathogen; this helps white blood cells to destroy it. Each type of antibody fits only one type of antigen, so this response is specific.

Third, white blood cells produce antitoxins. Some bacteria release toxins that damage tissues. Antitoxins bind to these toxins and neutralise them, so they can no longer cause harm. Producing the right antibodies takes time the first time a pathogen is met, which is why we feel ill while the white blood cells respond. When the infection is beaten, the person recovers.
keyFacts: Non-specific defences act against all pathogens and try to stop them entering the body.
Skin is a physical barrier and secretes antimicrobial substances.
The nose has hairs and mucus that trap particles that may contain pathogens.
The trachea and bronchi secrete mucus to trap pathogens; cilia move the mucus up to the throat to be swallowed.
The stomach produces hydrochloric acid, which kills pathogens.
If a pathogen enters the body, the immune system tries to destroy it.
White blood cells defend the body by phagocytosis, antibody production and antitoxin production.
Antibodies are specific: each binds to one type of antigen.
Antitoxins neutralise the toxins produced by bacteria.

keyTerms.definition: A defence that works against all pathogens, such as the skin, mucus and stomach acid.
Tiny hair-like structures on cells lining the trachea and bronchi that beat to move mucus up to the throat.
A sticky substance secreted in the nose, trachea and bronchi that traps pathogens and particles.
The process by which a white blood cell engulfs and digests a pathogen.
A protein produced by white blood cells that binds to a specific antigen on a pathogen, helping to destroy it.
A molecule (usually a protein) on the surface of a pathogen that is recognised by the immune system.
A substance produced by white blood cells that binds to and neutralises a toxin.
The body's system, including white blood cells, that destroys pathogens that have entered the body.

workedExamples.title: Explaining the defence in the airways
workedExamples.question: Explain how the trachea and bronchi stop pathogens reaching the lungs.
steps: Cells lining the trachea and bronchi secrete mucus.
The sticky mucus traps pathogens and dust in the air breathed in.
Ciliated cells have cilia that beat and move the mucus upwards to the throat.
The mucus is swallowed, and acid in the stomach kills the pathogens.
workedExamples.answer: Mucus traps pathogens and cilia waft the mucus up to the throat to be swallowed, so pathogens do not reach the lungs.

workedExamples.title: Three roles of white blood cells
workedExamples.question: Describe three ways in which white blood cells defend the body against a bacterium that produces a toxin.
steps: Phagocytosis: a white blood cell engulfs the bacterium and digests it.
Antibody production: antibodies bind to the specific antigens on the bacterium, helping white blood cells destroy it.
Antitoxin production: antitoxins bind to the toxin and neutralise it.
workedExamples.answer: Phagocytosis, antibodies that bind to the bacterium's antigens, and antitoxins that neutralise its toxin.

workedExamples.title: Calculation from blood count data
workedExamples.question: A blood sample contains 7500 white blood cells per mm³. 4500 of these are phagocytes. Calculate the percentage of white blood cells that are phagocytes.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think cilia trap pathogens.
misconceptions.right: In fact mucus traps pathogens; cilia beat to move the mucus up to the throat.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think antibodies kill pathogens by eating them.
misconceptions.right: In fact phagocytosis is done by white blood cells. Antibodies bind to specific antigens on pathogens, helping white blood cells to destroy them.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think one antibody works against every pathogen.
misconceptions.right: In fact antibodies are specific: each type binds only to one particular antigen.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often confuse antibodies and antitoxins.
misconceptions.right: In fact antibodies bind to antigens on pathogens, while antitoxins bind to and neutralise toxins released by bacteria.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the stomach acid digests pathogens with enzymes.
misconceptions.right: In fact the hydrochloric acid in the stomach kills pathogens.

realWorld: Smoking damages cilia in the airways, so mucus builds up and smokers suffer more chest infections.
Burns that destroy large areas of skin leave patients at high risk of infection, so they are treated in sterile conditions.
Blood tests that count white blood cells help doctors spot infections, as the count rises when the body is fighting a pathogen.
Antitoxin injections are used to treat some bacterial infections, such as tetanus, by neutralising the toxin.
examTips: Learn the four non-specific defences in order of the spec: skin, nose, trachea and bronchi, stomach, with what each does.
Do not say cilia 'catch' or 'trap' pathogens. Mucus traps; cilia move the mucus.
Name all three white blood cell roles precisely: phagocytosis, antibody production, antitoxin production.
When describing antibodies, use the words 'specific' and 'antigen' to access higher marks.
summary: Non-specific defences stop pathogens entering: skin, nose, trachea and bronchi, stomach.
Skin is a barrier and secretes antimicrobial substances.
Mucus traps pathogens; cilia move mucus to the throat; stomach acid kills pathogens.
The immune system destroys pathogens that get into the body.
White blood cells use phagocytosis, antibodies and antitoxins.
Antibodies are specific to antigens; antitoxins neutralise toxins.

options: To move mucus up to the throat
markScheme: 1 mark: to move mucus up to the throat
questions.explanation: Mucus traps pathogens; cilia beat to move the mucus up to the throat where it is swallowed. Cilia do not trap, digest or make antibodies.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT one of the ways white blood cells defend the body?
markScheme: 1 mark: producing hydrochloric acid
questions.explanation: Hydrochloric acid is produced by the stomach, a non-specific defence. White blood cells carry out phagocytosis and produce antibodies and antitoxins.

questions.question: How does the skin help to defend the body?
options: It acts as a physical barrier to pathogens
It produces antibodies on its surface
It contains cilia that move pathogens away
markScheme: 1 mark: it acts as a physical barrier
questions.explanation: The skin is a physical barrier and also secretes antimicrobial substances. Cilia are found in the airways and acid in the stomach.

questions.question: What is phagocytosis?
options: Producing proteins that bind to toxins
A white blood cell engulfing and digesting a pathogen
Mucus trapping dust in the nose
markScheme: 1 mark: a white blood cell engulfing and digesting a pathogen
questions.explanation: Phagocytosis means a white blood cell surrounds (engulfs) a pathogen and digests it. Binding to toxins describes antitoxins.

questions.question: What is the function of an antitoxin?
options: To bind to antigens on viruses
To neutralise toxins produced by bacteria
markScheme: 1 mark: to neutralise toxins produced by bacteria
questions.explanation: Antitoxins bind to toxins and neutralise them. Antibodies bind to antigens, and engulfing is phagocytosis.

questions.question: Which pair correctly matches a part of the body with how it prevents pathogens entering?
markScheme: 1 mark: trachea: mucus traps pathogens
questions.explanation: The trachea and bronchi secrete mucus that traps pathogens. The other options mix up the defences: acid is in the stomach, hairs are in the nose and cilia are in the airways.

questions.question: Why can an antibody against the measles virus not protect against the bacterium that causes Salmonella food poisoning?
options: Antibodies only work on bacteria, not viruses
Antibodies are specific and bind only to the antigen they match
Salmonella bacteria are destroyed only by stomach acid
Antibodies are only produced in children
markScheme: 1 mark: antibodies are specific to one antigen
questions.explanation: Each antibody has a shape that fits one particular antigen. The measles antibody does not fit the antigens on Salmonella, so it cannot bind to it.

questions.question: Smoking stops cilia from working. Which is the most likely result?
options: Mucus builds up in the airways and more pathogens reach the lungs, causing more chest infections
Smokers produce more hydrochloric acid in the stomach
The skin becomes a better physical barrier
White blood cells can no longer carry out phagocytosis anywhere in the body
markScheme: 1 mark: mucus builds up and more pathogens reach the lungs
questions.explanation: Without working cilia, mucus containing trapped pathogens is not moved up to the throat, so it collects in the airways and pathogens can infect the lungs.

questions.question: Which cells in the blood help to defend the body against pathogens?
markScheme: 1 mark: white blood cells
questions.explanation: White blood cells are part of the immune system. Red blood cells carry oxygen and platelets help blood clot; ciliated cells line the airways rather than the blood.

questions.question: A person has an infection caused by a bacterium that releases a toxin. Which response by white blood cells would reduce tissue damage from the toxin most directly?
markScheme: 1 mark: producing antitoxins
questions.explanation: Antitoxins bind to and neutralise toxins, so the toxin can no longer damage tissues. The other options do not act on the toxin.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the number of red blood cells and white blood cells in a blood sample.
Calculate the ratio of red blood cells to white blood cells.
Give your answer in the form x : 1 to the nearest whole number.
questions.explanation: Divide the number of red blood cells by the number of white blood cells: 5 000 000 ÷ 7500 = 666.67, which rounds to 667. So there are about 667 red blood cells for every white blood cell.

questions.question: Describe how the nose helps to stop pathogens entering the body.
markScheme: 1 mark: hairs and/or mucus in the nose
1 mark: trap particles/pathogens
questions.explanation: Hairs and sticky mucus in the nose trap particles in the air that may contain pathogens.

questions.question: Name the three ways in which white blood cells help to defend the body against pathogens.
markScheme: 1 mark: phagocytosis
1 mark: producing antibodies
1 mark: producing antitoxins
questions.explanation: These are the three methods listed in the specification.

questions.question: Explain how the stomach helps to defend the body against pathogens.
markScheme: 1 mark: the stomach produces hydrochloric acid
1 mark: which kills pathogens (swallowed in food, drink or mucus)
questions.explanation: Acid conditions kill most pathogens that are swallowed.

questions.question: Describe how the trachea and bronchi prevent pathogens reaching the lungs.
markScheme: 1 mark: cells secrete mucus
1 mark: mucus traps pathogens
1 mark: cilia move/waft the mucus up to the throat (to be swallowed)
questions.explanation: Mucus traps; cilia move. Both are needed for full marks.

questions.question: Explain how antibodies help to destroy a pathogen.
markScheme: 1 mark: antibodies bind to (specific) antigens on the pathogen
1 mark: which helps white blood cells to destroy the pathogen
questions.explanation: Antibodies attach to antigens on the pathogen's surface; this marks it out and helps white blood cells destroy it.

questions.question: Suggest why a person with a large burn to the skin is at high risk of infection.
markScheme: 1 mark: the skin, a physical barrier, has been damaged or lost
1 mark: so pathogens can enter the body more easily
questions.explanation: Without intact skin, the first line of defence is lost and pathogens can enter the tissues directly.

acceptedAnswers: white blood cells slow to respond
markScheme: 1 mark: it takes time for white blood cells to produce the correct (specific) antibodies
1 mark: meanwhile the pathogen reproduces and causes symptoms
questions.explanation: The first time a pathogen is met, the right antibodies are not ready, so the pathogen has time to reproduce and cause illness.

questions.question: What is meant by an antigen?
markScheme: 1 mark: a molecule (protein) on the surface of a pathogen (that antibodies bind to)
questions.explanation: Antigens are surface molecules that the immune system recognises.

questions.question: Describe the non-specific defences of the human body and how each one stops pathogens causing infection.
markScheme: Indicative content: skin: physical barrier; secretes antimicrobial substances; nose: hairs and mucus trap particles containing pathogens; trachea and bronchi: secrete mucus that traps pathogens; cilia beat to move mucus up to the throat where it is swallowed; stomach: produces hydrochloric acid which kills pathogens; these act against all pathogens and stop them entering the body.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): all four defences described with a clear explanation of how each one works.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): three or four defences described with some explanation, or two in detail.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one or two defences named with little explanation.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: For full marks describe skin, nose, trachea and bronchi, and stomach, and explain how each prevents pathogens getting in or kills them.

questions.question: Explain how white blood cells defend the body against a bacterium that has entered through a cut and produces a toxin.
markScheme: Indicative content: immune system tries to destroy the pathogen; phagocytosis: white blood cells engulf and digest the bacteria; antibody production: white blood cells make antibodies specific to antigens on the bacteria; antibodies bind to antigens, helping destroy them; antitoxin production: antitoxins bind to and neutralise the toxin so it cannot damage tissues.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): clear explanation of all three mechanisms linked to the bacterium and its toxin.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): names one or more mechanisms with limited explanation.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: All three mechanisms are relevant here: phagocytosis and antibodies act on the bacterium, and antitoxins act on its toxin.

questions.question: Compare the non-specific defence systems with the role of white blood cells in defending the body.
markScheme: Indicative content: non-specific defences act against all pathogens; they try to stop pathogens entering (skin, mucus in nose and airways, cilia, stomach acid); white blood cells act once a pathogen has entered the body; phagocytosis is also non-specific; antibodies and antitoxins are specific to a particular antigen or toxin; antibody production takes time on first infection, whereas barriers are always present.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): clear comparison with at least one similarity and differences in where and how each works.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): describes one system or gives simple unlinked points.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: The key difference is that barriers prevent entry and act against everything, while antibody and antitoxin production targets specific pathogens or toxins after entry.
